comments.body:
@afranck 
I could use help with this one too if you know it.
This is not Pisonia aculeata. Note that the thorns are joined at the base and do not curve as in P. aculeata. Also, the leaves and branching pattern are not a match.
stumped at the moment, very curious

That might be a first. All I can say from my personal experience so far is that it hurts a bit to maneuver through, but not even close to the level of Pisonia aculeata, which I take much greater care to avoid touching.

https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/142378141

This is a really good example showing how the main trunk thorns (much larger than the thorns on the branches) grow from start to finish. Clearly, the bullhorn thorn is how they begin their journey, and then they sprout more thorns over time, eventually becoming a semicircle of spines.

Thanks @andresvila
The leaves seem to match. Especially in https://www.inaturalist.org/photos/56324059?size=original

I was looking through other Pereskia aculeata observations in Miami and you have the only two! (including this one).
Looking through different RG observations, it does seem like a match.
Check out the thorn pattern and leaves in the second photo of this one: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/142378141

See photo 1 and 4 https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/142131678
Photo 4 is extremely similar to yours.

Those glochidia of spines are what make it so nasty
Glochidia are absent in Pereskia. Do you mean something else?
What is the correct term then, for the clusters of spines on the older stems? Thought it was the same as those on other cactuses.
Thank you. Better to describe structures rather than use terms incorrectly :-(

Areoles are the reduced shoots that originate in the axils of leaves and don't elongate into proper shoots. These bear various structures, in this case spines, in other cases hairs, and only in the subfamily Opuntioideae they bear glochidia, with or without spines.
